what.heading: What happened
paras: Imagine a college generating thousands of certificates. One wrong entry shouldn't ruin the batch or crash the service. <hi>Bas itna hi kaam tha.</hi>
I mapped the workflow and architecture, made or approved product decisions, and used AI coding tools to implement the prototype. The prototype passed **324 tests**.
A separate audit found **19 problems**: one input consumed excessive processing time; another ballooned into an enormous response. <hi>Tests ne woh sawaal poochhe hi nahi the.</hi>

next.heading: <hi>Maine phir kya kiya</hi>
paras: <hi>Green screen pe ruk jaana aasaan tha.</hi> **I didn't defend the green screen.** Records show me approving safeguards, changing scope and directing more remediation when problems remained. Agents audited and fixed the code. The final report recorded zero open findings in its scope; later checks passed **479 main and 232 audit tests**.

warning.heading: Fair warning
paras: It's still a prototype, not a security guarantee. <hi>Isse zyaada ka daava main nahi karta.</hi>

stop.hook: The prototype passed 324 tests. A separate audit found 19 problems.
stop.next: <hi>Green screen par ruk jaana aasaan tha.</hi> I didn't defend it: records show me approving safeguards and directing more remediation.
stop.warning: Still a prototype, not a security guarantee.
stop.twin: 324 of 324 tests passed. A separate audit then found 19 problems, two of them high.

lamps.kicker: LAMP 2 · VIGIL · THE WATCHDOG THAT TRUSTED A LATE REPLY
lamps.title: <hi>Der se aaya jawab</hi>
lamps.lit: <hi>Lamp 2 jal utha. Ek diya jala. Ab agla.</hi>

what.heading: What happened
paras: Vigil checked whether a data connection was alive, <hi>jaise phone par poochhna: "Hello? Aap wahin hain?"</hi>
Despite green tests, a reply arriving **after the deadline** could count as proof of health. <hi>Der se aaya jawab bhi "haan, zinda hoon" maan liya ja sakta tha.</hi>

next.heading: <hi>Maine phir kya kiya</hi>
paras: <hi>Maine ek sawaal uthaya: kya yeh tests system ka asli vaada sach mein check karte hain?</hi>
I questioned whether the tests proved the system's real promise. An AI-assisted review found the defect and implemented an approval-gated correction.
When a verifier removed the correction, **two targeted tests failed**. Restored, the suite passed **105 tests**.
The question became: **does it deliver what someone depends on?**

warning.heading: Fair warning
paras: <hi>Yeh sab simulated connections par hua tha.</hi> The 105 tests were verified locally in an agent session, not in CI, and there was no production deployment.

voice.heading: <hi>Soch poori hone do</hi>
paras: Here's a real thought I spoke on **2 November 2026**: "Shouldn't the technology adapt to how we naturally think and communicate?"
<hi>Dono ko saath rakh ke padhiye: meri hand-transcribed voice memo, aur Flow ka actual text. Thought wahi raha; bas expression saaf ho gaya.</hi>
That matters more to me than "type faster": **let people finish thinking.**
voice.gatedBuildLine: I spoke some of the directions for this page through Wispr Flow into Emergent. Flow transcribed me; Emergent built the page; I looked at what it made and dictated a correction. The before and after are linked here.

compare.instruction: <hi>Flame ko meri awaaz se Flow ke text tak khiskaiye.</hi> (Arrow keys work too, or use "Read it plainly".)
compare.legend: Blue pencil: words Flow trimmed. Highlighted: words Flow smoothed or added.
compare.altText: Two columns of text for each take, my spoken words on the left and Flow's text on the right, joined by a glowing line.

takes.label: Take 1
raw: Okay, so... the best interface... I think it's basically when you don't have to think about using it, like learning it sorry sorry how to use it.
Like, when you're using something and you're not constantly wondering where to click or what to do next.
You're just... doing what you came there to do.
And, yeah, I think that's actually quite difficult to build. Because all the complicated stuff, the logic, the decisions... someone has to handle all of that. Just not the user.
takes.out: Okay the best interface, I think, is basically when you don't have to think about how to use it, like when you are using something and you are not constantly wondering where to click or what to do next. You are just doing what you came there to do. I think that's actually quite difficult to build because all the complicated stuff, the logic, the decisions, someone has to handle all of that, just not the user.

takes.label: Take 2
raw: Wait, I think there's another way to look at this.
We spend so much time learning how to use technology... remembering commands, figuring out buttons, changing ourselves to fit the tool adjusting to how a tool works.
But why? I mean, shouldn't it be the other way around?
Shouldn't the technology adapt to how we naturally think and communicate?
Because we already know what we want to say. We shouldn't have to learn the tool first struggle just to get it out.
takes.out: I think there's another way to look at this. We spend so much time learning how to use technology: remembering commands, figuring out buttons, adjusting to how a tool works. But why? Shouldn't it be the other way around? Shouldn't the technology adapt to how we naturally think and communicate? Because we already know what we want to say, we shouldn't have to struggle just to get it out.

evidence.title: Evidence drawer
evidence.intro: Every figure on this page has a source and a status. Statuses are plain text: PUBLIC, LOCAL-BRANCH, REPO-REPORTED, PERSONALLY CONFIRMED, UNRESOLVED, PROPOSED. <hi>Koi ek claim chuniye, evidence kholiye. Jahan jawab abhi adhura hai, wahan UNRESOLVED likha hai.</hi>

folders.name: CERTGEN: The green wall
folders.blurb: <hi>324 tests, phir 19 findings, aur mera hissa kitna tha.</hi>

body.purpose: A college can generate certificates for thousands of students, accept the valid rows and explain the invalid rows without making everyone else start again.
body.finding: 324 passing release-candidate tests preceded a separate 19-finding forensic audit (two high). Among the issues were disproportionate CPU work on a crafted value and memory-intensive expansion from a roughly 26 MB request into roughly 192 MB of response material. The audit did not certify the prototype for unrestricted network exposure.
body.mine: Requirements and architectural decisions were recorded. I approved bounded error-reporting, resource limits, later authentication-related changes and continuing remediation when findings remained. AI agents performed many of the technical investigations and fixes.
body.results: The remediation report says zero open findings within the identified list. Later local checks passed 479 main-suite and 232 audit-suite tests (separate suites, not necessarily 711 independent tests). The optional QR-verification branch passed its own tests but failed a pre-agreed existing requirement and was not merged. A series of further remediation attempts was necessary, and no claim of security certification is justified.

inspect.label: Bulk Certificate Generator
inspect.note: Some of these reports are local or ignored in the repository. For those, the evidence is available on request.

status: Test counts, audit and remediation results
Some report files are local or ignored in the repository
more: “The Feature I Killed”: a QR enhancement was rejected because it regressed required PDF behavior. This is a scope and quality judgment, not a statement about the feature's inherent worth.
Commit trailers credit autonomous AI work. I did not personally write every endpoint.

folders.name: VIGIL: The late witness
folders.blurb: <hi>Ek late reply, ek sawaal, aur do tests jo correction hatane par fail hue.</hi>

body.purpose: A monitor checks whether a stream of important information is still alive. A late reply must not count as proof of current health.
body.finding: The original handle_pong logic accepted stale or future-timestamped replies. The project plan records a question about whether its tests truly established the stated state-machine behavior. An agent investigated the code and implemented the correction with an approval gate.
body.mine: I questioned whether the tests proved the system's real promise.
body.results: A later local verification reported 105/105 tests passing. Replacing the guard with `if (false)` made exactly two targeted tests fail. A simulated three-feed lifecycle demonstrated failure, reconnection and recovery. There was no production exchange deployment, and the kernel-level network-loss script was not run.
status: 105/105 tests, verified locally in an agent session (not CI)
Who asked the correctness question and who approved the semantic change
more: A CLI dropped piped commands when EOF arrived with the final input; the pattern appeared at three sites.
A benchmark comparing reactor architectures inherited a one-CPU affinity mask, invalidating the original naive-baseline comparison. Committed documents still disagree on absolute CPU numbers.
An 18-gap specification exercise led to a first-class feed simulator and protocol decisions.
One deeper fuzzing harness hung in the sandbox and remains incompletely validated. None of this is production or CI evidence.

folders.name: BLITZ: The number I withdrew
folders.blurb: <hi>1,205 se 1,850 tak ka poora hisaab, aur jo abhi remeasure nahi hua.</hi>

body.purpose: A fast matching engine keeps track of buyers and sellers, but a claimed speed improvement matters only if it can be reliably reproduced.
body.finding: The README's earlier 1,205 ns headline came from an uncommitted working tree. A more controlled historical run gave 1,850 ns. A reported memory-layout advantage shrank from 3.1× to about 1.02× and some verdicts became inconclusive.
body.mine: The decision to retract or downgrade the claim is visible in commit f46a9cb and in historical README revisions. AI agents were involved in the benchmark overhaul and the audits.
body.results: A later AI-executed audit found 3,059 crossed-at-rest states in 110,000 replay events (2.78%). Remediation reported zero such states on the replay, and fixing the matching engine made earlier latency numbers stale. New engine latency was not remeasured. An existing test had actually asserted the invalid state.
status: Current latency has not been remeasured. The 1,850 ns run is historical.
more: At last review, the public default branch did not include the stale-results warning.
An AF_XDP latency spike was traced to competing processes pinned to the same cores and touchpad interrupts; that subsystem has since been removed from uncommitted work.
A chart displayed passing tests despite missing executables and an unverified sanitizer claim.
An Avellaneda–Stoikov strategy lost to a naive benchmark on five tickers; the reason for reverting it is not documented.

folders.name: TIPINDEX: The operator changed, the evidence stayed
folders.blurb: <hi>Handoff ka record, aur woh jawab jo abhi UNRESOLVED hain.</hi>

body.purpose: Instead of searching every market message, an index can jump to relevant ones, but that shortcut has maintenance and workload costs.
body.finding: During a P6 measurement campaign Codex ran out of usage allowance, a process died, and one output file was truncated. I redirected the work to Claude Code, controlled progress and approved deleting checksum-verified redundant chunks to recover disk. Agents verified checkpoint integrity; the reports state 820 measured rounds and that 5,364 original P6 files remained byte-identical.
body.mine: The project records explicit phase gates, selection of a narrower Tier B plan, stop and start instructions, approval of controlled deletions, the switch from Codex to Claude Code, and permission to remediate audit findings. Most C++ and Python development, benchmarking and audit execution was agent-written.
body.results: In a separate P7 runtime study, CPU contamination invalidated 9 of 10 rounds in attempt one; a new quiescence rule rejected attempt two at 3.52 seconds against a 3.0-second limit; attempt three passed. The rule was written after attempt one but before the reruns. Failed timing values were deleted at my instruction, despite a general “preserve failures” policy.
status: Understanding of the generated code: needs a genuine walkthrough. An October interview-prep prompt in the repository states I had zero working knowledge of it at that moment.
more: Two audits found 26 and then 14 numbered findings; the mutation audit showed three no-op invariant checkers could pass the existing tests.
A polling-budget feature shortened individual turns but increased cumulative work and retained unresolved overhead.
These are one-laptop, limited-workload results, not generalized product speedups. The P7 contamination and the P6 agent interruption are distinct campaigns.

folders.name: PITDB: The future appeared early
folders.blurb: <hi>06:15, 06:00 par: kya local branch par hai, aur kya public par.</hi>

body.purpose: A historical database should answer “What was actually known by this point in time?” without quietly using later facts.
body.finding: One specific direct-ingestion daylight-saving-time fold could make a 06:15 UTC record visible at a 06:00 UTC cutoff. The normalized UTC CSV route was not affected. Agent-executed remediation centralized timestamp validation and rejected problematic input.

folders.name: INDIA GROWTH TEST: The proposed protocol

fields: Test whether a setup script for the family member who installs Flow on an older relative's phone (Hinglish on, their people's names added, first dictation a real message to someone they love) makes that relative dictate again on their own, after the helper has left the room.

Pairs of a young helper (18 to 25) and a relative (parent, grandparent, aunt or uncle) who writes Hindi or Hinglish on WhatsApp, on an Android 13+ phone or an iPhone, free plan. A, Speed demo (control): the helper installs with default settings, says "Mummy, ye typing se kaafi tez hai. Bolke dekhiye.", the relative dictates a test sentence, the helper leaves. B, Handover script: the helper picks Hinglish in the language setting on the relative's own phone, adds five names that matter to the relative to the personal dictionary, and says "Mummy, ek message boliye jo aap Aarav ko bhejna chahti hain."; the text appears in Latin letters, the helper checks the names, the relative sends it in WhatsApp; the helper then leaves the room and the house for that session. Both arms: same phone mix, same follow-up card, same consent, same leave step. B bundles three changes (Hinglish, names, real message); a pilot cannot separate them.

12 dyads (6 and 6, assigned by coin flip), one week plus a day-7 call. Exploratory only. No significance claims. Twelve dyads cannot show cause; they can show whether the idea is worth real instrumentation.

Primary: a first usable dictation (sent in a real chat with at most one small fix), then an unassisted second dictation within 24 hours of the first, when the helper was not in the room. Secondary: any unassisted dictation on day 7; names right on first try, out of the five; helper minutes spent on setup; total words in 7 days, descriptive only. Guardrails: any language setting changed away from Hinglish (and why); any weekly limit message seen; discomfort or "bahut mushkil hai" feedback; helper stress; any privacy concern. Any guardrail breach in B is reported first.

With consent: the sent message arriving in the family chat (timestamp), the relative's one-tap answer ("bola ya type kiya?"), a photo of the Flow history or statistics screen where the app shows one, and a 3-question check by call on day 1 and day 7. I will not read chats or hold audio. No Wispr data is used.

Scale (to about 40 dyads, or hand the script to Wispr as a spec): B has at least 4 of 6 unassisted second dictations AND at least 2 more dyads than A. Change: B leads by exactly 1, or ties on the primary but is clearly better on names or day-7; re-cut the script and rerun. Kill this version: A equals or beats B on the primary, or B has any guardrail breach.
About ₹2,000 to ₹2,500: thank-you snacks for 12 dyads about ₹1,800, a printed one-page setup card and follow-up about ₹200, data and travel about ₹300. Free plan only; nobody is asked to pay.

Helper skill differs across dyads. People try harder when watched. Novelty in week one. Older users may stop for reasons unrelated to the script. Free-plan limits could hit mid-week. Consent: informed, spoken-and-written consent in the participant's language; adults only; free to stop any time; no audio recording; data deleted after the write-up.
status: The Handover Test. No result, lift, sample or Wispr data is claimed. Neither experiment has been run.

sixty.label: THE 60-SECOND FILE
sixty.headline: 324 tests passed. A separate audit found 19 problems. Would you have shipped it?
paras: Namaste. I'm Shriniwas, an engineering student applying to Wispr Flow's India growth internship. I mapped workflows and architectures, made or approved key design decisions, and used AI agents for implementation and investigation.

In one project, I approved further corrections after the first audit fixes weren't enough. In another, a watchdog called a late reply proof of a healthy connection; I questioned whether the tests actually proved the product's promise, and the corrected test failed when its fix was removed.
I also withdrew a flattering speed claim, redirected an interrupted experiment between AI agents, and narrowed a database claim after a specific time-handling defect.

I have no growth wins to borrow. But I've used Flow, and I want to test what happens after the helper leaves the room: when a younger relative sets Flow up for an older one, does the older person dictate again, alone, the next day? Proposed, not run.
sixty.pull: I can't promise I'll always be right. I can show you what I do when I'm wrong.

steps.t: TipIndex: a quiet-machine rule, limit 3.0 s, written after attempt one but before the reruns. certgen: the QR branch was held to a pre-agreed requirement and not merged.

certgen: 324 tests, then 19 audit findings. Vigil: swap the guard for `if (false)` and exactly two targeted tests fail. Blitz: 3,059 crossed-at-rest states in 110,000 replay events.

India test: a setup script for the family member who installs Flow on a relative's phone, measured by whether the relative dictates again alone within 24 hours; success defined in advance. Proposed, not run.

growth.card: Mera experiment: The Handover Test (Haath Chhodke Dekho). Variant A is a speed demo. Variant B: the helper picks Hinglish by hand on the relative's own phone, adds five names that matter to the relative to the personal dictionary, and the first dictation is a real message to someone they love. Then the helper leaves the room. The question: does the relative dictate again, alone, within a day? Twelve family pairs, six per arm, one week, exploratory only. The rule is fixed in advance: scale only if B gets at least 4 of 6 and beats A by at least 2; otherwise change or kill. Cost about ₹2,000. Proposed, not run.
growth.why: Why this is my idea, not a template: A template would say "test two pitches". This tests what happens after the helper walks away.
growth.limits: Honest limits: Proposed, not run. I have never owned a growth channel. Twelve pairs cannot show cause, and I have no Wispr data. The "India onboarding" angle is my hypothesis, not something Wispr has said.
